content:
Introducing The Cold Soak, a podcast where we discuss what’s been happening in South African wine over the past month – new releases, industry chatter, bold moves and questionable decisions.

Hosted by Ex Animo Wine Co.’s David Clarke and Winemag.co.za editor Christian Eedes, it pairs two informed, independent voices with a clear sense of perspective.

Each episode cuts through the noise: key releases, sharp takes on Winemag reports, and candid discussion on where the industry is headed.

The approach is rigorous but unpretentious, analytical with a touch of humour – equally relevant to industry insiders and engaged drinkers alike.

Listen to the latest review here.

title: Malu Lambert: Noordhoek emerges as a Cape wine destination
summary:
It’s been essential for me, as a wine writer, to live outside the boundaries of the winelands. Were I to live in say, Stellenbosch, I would quickly become overwhelmed. For all its pretence of laid-backness, working in wine is anything but. There is a constant stream of tastings, events, farm visits, and somewhere in between […]

The post Malu Lambert: Noordhoek emerges as a Cape wine destination appeared first on winemag.
content:
It’s been essential for me, as a wine writer, to live outside the boundaries of the winelands. Were I to live in say, Stellenbosch, I would quickly become overwhelmed. For all its pretence of laid-backness, working in wine is anything but. There is a constant stream of tastings, events, farm visits, and somewhere in between it all I’ve got to get down to the actual writing, which, as a freelancer, is an endless juggle.

Living in Noordhoek, a beautiful coastal suburb at the foot of Chapman’s Peak, gives me a sense of remove; a place to retreat (behind the lentil curtain, as it were). But here’s the thing: we do have a wine culture here, and it’s growing.

Cape Point Vineyards, on the slopes of Chapman’s Peak, has long been the castle, towering over the small community famed for its cult sauv-sem blend, Isliedh. The first vintage circa 2003, made by Duncan Savage who left after 14-years to start his own label. He still has an affinity for the deep south, with Girl Next Door sourced from syrah vineyards in both Fish Hoek and Noordhoek.

The future of Cape Point Vineyards, however, hangs somewhat in the balance. What began as a commercial disagreement between founder Sybrand van der Spuy and businessman Stephen Newton, who acquired much of the property for his Alexander Estate, has escalated into multiple court cases and allegations of intimidation. One incident made mainstream news: Van der Spuy was alleged to have threatened staff with what they believed was a firearm, a claim he denied, maintaining that the object was in fact a pepper-ball launcher.

 

Just below Cape Point Vineyards find Alexander Estate, a winery and boutique luxury hotel. The land had once belonged to Newton’s grandfather, Alexander Newton, who lost it after an unsuccessful attempt at farming following his retirement as a boilermaker. In bringing it back into the family, Newton has also saved the vineyards from a proposed housing development. “That would have been a disaster for Noordhoek,” says CEO and cellarmaster Hannes Meyer, who also continues to oversee winemaking at Cape Point Vineyards. “It would have stripped away so much of what makes this place special.”

The newly launched Alexander range features both estate-grown as well as wines Meyer has sourced fruit for. The standout is the proudly Noordhoek, Susara 2024: a blend of sauvignon blanc, sémillon and sauvignon gris, the latter bringing a distinct savouriness and texture to the blend with its tiny berries, and wind-battered thick skins.

“We want this to be a brand the valley feels a part of,” he says. “Something that gives back.”

Community is something Noordhoek does well. The Farm Village is its beating heart, home to the yoga studio where you’ll usually find me, a coffee roastery, juice bar and, of course, one of the country’s best wine restaurants, The Foodbarn. Franck Dangereux’s offering includes his own label with some of his ‘wine friends’, including names like Silverthorn, Trizanne Barnard and Catherine Marshall.

While down Beach Road, Furny’s Wine Bar manages to cram a spectacular and varied selection onto very limited shelf space. In the same milkwood-enclosed compound is the Aegir Project Brewery, South Africa’s best craft brewery, in my opinion anyway. They have a cracking wine list too, and owner Rory Lancellas releases a collaboration once a year with his winemaker friends, Ode to the Harvest, bottle-conditioned saison aged in wine barrels.

It’s here, one fine day, with the blue arc of the Atlantic visible through the upstairs windows, that Noordhoeker, Natasha Jacka is presenting her latest Alinea releases.

After working as a chef Jacka started to get curious about wine. On a whim she decided to join the harvest team at Cape Point Vineyards in 2017. A pivotal moment came on the bottling line when Riandri Visser, who succeeded Savage as winemaker, handed Jacka a bottle and said, ‘This is yours. You made this.’ “I knew then that this was what I wanted to do for the rest of my life.” She enrolled at Elsenburg, graduated top of her class in 2020, and launched Alinea the following year.

At home during lockdown she was looking out over her mother’s horse paddocks, and the idea came to her to plant some vines. “My mom, dad, sister and I dug every hole ourselves, planted every vine and put in every stake.” Three years after establishing the vineyard, the first fruit was harvested in 2024. The first block comprised 750 stok-by-paaltjie syrah vines, followed by a six-variety white field blend of just 650 vines (read reviews of the latest releases here).

Jacka describes Noordhoek as ‘one of the Cape’s coolest and windiest pockets’ with annual rainfall typically between 600 and 900mm.

Just down the road, outside Kommetjie, she is involved in another project at the landmark Imhoff Farm, where echalas vines were planted in 2019. The 1.5-hectares are planted to chardonnay, pinot noir and shiraz and occupy a north-east-facing slope overlooking Long Beach towards Chapman’s Peak. “The planting method and cultivars were chosen for the windy conditions,” says consulting viticulturist Hendri Burger. “They flower before the south-easterly winds arrive.” The vineyard is farmed organically.

It’s been reported that the establishment of the Kommetjie Vineyard Estate forms part of a long-term vision to create a Peninsula wine route. Which leaves me with one small problem: it seems the winelands have finally caught up with me.

  • Malu Lambert is a freelance wine journalist and wine judge who has written for numerous local and international titles. She is a WSET Diploma alum and won the title of Louis Roederer Emerging Wine Writer of the Year 2019, among many other accolades. She sits on various tasting panels and has judged in competitions abroad. Follow her on X: @MaluLambert

title: Last chance to enter the Aspiring Top Drop Awards 2026
summary:
Entries for the inaugural Top Drop Awards sponsored by courier company Aspiring are now open. To be eligible, a wine must retail for R120 a bottle or less, either at the producer’s cellar door or through a major retailer such as Checkers, Pick n Pay, Makro, TOPS at SPAR or Woolworths. How results will be […]

The post Last chance to enter the Aspiring Top Drop Awards 2026 appeared first on winemag.
content:
Entries for the inaugural Top Drop Awards sponsored by courier company Aspiring are now open. To be eligible, a wine must retail for R120 a bottle or less, either at the producer’s cellar door or through a major retailer such as Checkers, Pick n Pay, Makro, TOPS at SPAR or Woolworths.

How results will be communicated

On the website, we balance quality (points) and value. To achieve this, we publish both 100-point scores and a derived value score.

Value Score = Quality Points × (Reference Price / Wine Price)

The higher the quality and the lower the price relative to the reference, the higher the value score.

In-store, we simplify to a single consumer cue. All wines at R120 or under that meet the selection threshold receive the same badge. The aim is clarity: one mark of approval signalling quality, affordability and trust, without score comparison or visual clutter.

Judges

Awards chairman is Winemag.co.za editor Christian Eedes. Judges are:

Robin Kenny, DipWSET
Malu Lambert, wine writer
Francois Rautenbach, hospitality and wine specialist
Lauren Segers, Brice & Burnett
Suné van der Merwe, wine consultant
Tarryn Vincent, Reciprocal Wine Company

Enter now

Entries close on Wednesday 29 July. For the rules and entry form, click here.

Prizes

The producer of the best wine overall in each of the respective categories wins shipping services worth R5 000 from Aspiring Couriers.

title: Tim James: Varietal wines, mono-varietals, and multi-blends
summary:
Questions around the blending of grape varieties have been milling around in my mind this past week, prompted by a comment and query on my article about the latest Sadie releases. There are four wines in the range that have large numbers of varieties in their make-up: the two Signature wines (Columella with 7; Palladius […]

The post Tim James: Varietal wines, mono-varietals, and multi-blends appeared first on winemag.
content:
Questions around the blending of grape varieties have been milling around in my mind this past week, prompted by a comment and query on my article about the latest Sadie releases. There are four wines in the range that have large numbers of varieties in their make-up: the two Signature wines (Columella with 7; Palladius with 15) and the two wines of the mixed vineyards on the home farm (red Songvang and white Twiswind with 12 grapes each). GillesP wondered whether such a blend “can actually reveal any specific personality in a wine expression?” He said: “As we are mostly used to blend of 2 to 4 varietals, it seems like a very diluting exercise”.

I enjoy questions that imply thought and promote me to both think and investigate. My response was basically to counterpose site expression to varietal expression, saying that this is what Sadie is after – in the blends and the monovarietal wines too. Incidentally, you’ll note that the Sadie wines made from just one or two varieties do not mention those on the labels, though there’s no secrecy: they are listed on the released wine notes. This label-silence is true for a number of modern producers that want to downplay varieties and stress vineyard origins – Alheit, Savage, David & Nadia, for example, but also others.

So I pointed out that a wine-lover concern with varieties is very much a modern one. Here I offer a few more observations on the matter, with some of my usual digressions.

As I suggested before, it’s interesting to notice an often substantial shift in the nature of vineyard plantings following the great turmoil initiated by the rampant vine diseases of the 19th century – firstly oidium, but most  importantly phylloxera in the century’s last decades. (Not that it is at all easy finding facts and figures about this; I’ve been trying; as usual, there’s a depressing lack of interest in wine history evident.) However, it’s clear that what we think to be the norm doesn’t often stretch much beyond modern times.

Take the most famous blend of all – red Bordeaux. Stephen Brook in his The Complete Bordeaux refers to 1794 records of 34 red varieties and 29 whites on the Right Bank, though fewer in the Médoc. Later, the most famous of the disappearing varieties was carmenère – thought to be extinct until it was identified in Chile, where they’d imported it thinking it to be merlot…. (Savvy Australia’s albariño import turned out to be savagnin; our own fondly imagined tempranillo turned out to be trincadeira – not to mention the infamous illegal smuggling of chardonnay which was in fact auxerrois; it’s clearly not hard to make such mistakes.)

In another example of crisis-prompted change, France’s Sancerre became overwhelmingly planted to sauvignon blanc, whereas it used to be mostly pinot noir and gamay; a little pinot remains, but gamay not – there also used to be a great deal more of this latter variety on the Côte d’Or. In Cognac the traditional variety until last century was folle blanche, but this is now in a tiny minority.

The same great varietal shift happened elsewhere too. In Galicia in Spain, for example, the response to financial pressures after upheavals led to the myriad indigenous varieties being replaced by other grapes – and, as widely in France, by hybrids (including American non-vinifera varieties) which didn’t need grafting onto rootstocks. Happily, this situation is now being reversed by quality-conscious producers.

The South African vineyard also looked very different as the 20th century emerged. A good thing, in fact, as an increased diversity replaced the former total dominance of semillon (greengrape). Syrah, sauvignon blanc, cabernet and – above all – cinsault (known then as hermitage) shouldered their way into the vineyards, amongst others.

Talking of South Africa, it’s always quite amusing to observe how, at tastings of some of the great mid-century red blends, admiring drinkers tend to be at a bit of a loss because we simply don’t know, in most cases, what varieties were included, let alone in what proportions (see here for some indication of how Chateau Libertas changed over the decades). It was clearly a much less important consideration back then than it is for us today, when we seem to need the hook of varietal knowledge for our understanding.

On which local note, a few incidentals: There were certainly Cape wines in the latter 19th century that were marketed with varietal names – a modernising touch, presumably intended to differentiate the wines from generic stuff hopefully and ridiculously called Moselle, Vin de Grave, Madeira, etc. I’ve seen labels mentioning Riesling (mistakenly!), Pontac, Greengrape. Secondly, I suspect that the Cape was surely a unique pioneer in the New World in having its best-known wine named for its genuine origin, Constantia. That’s something to be proud of.

The worldwide rise in varietal wines – that is, those primarily identified, especially on the label, by the grape variety or sometime varieties – was hugely promoted, if not invented, in America. Such varietalism was used by the UC Davis academic Maynard Amerine as a way of encouraging farmers to plant better varieties after the repeal of prohibition. The practice was later pushed in America by the writer Frank Schoonmaker and, says the Oxford Companion to Wine, ‘was embraced during the 1970s to distinguish the more ambitious wines, often made from Cabernet Sauvignon and, increasingly, Chardonnay, from the lack-lustre generics of old’. Such is the power of the USA that the practice spread – not least to South Africa, where it is also dominant.

I think that this varietalism, while it clearly had and has its uses, also has downsides. Basically, I suppose, it’s the reason we wine lovers are so besotted with knowing the grape variety, as a way of helping us respond to the wine. Partly because it tends to work like a brand. The first great example of this was the rise in chardonnay’s popularity, which also led to its being made primarily in one buttery, oaky style. It’s now rather like that with sauvignon blanc: it tends to all have a common set of identifiers, and those identifiers are pretty strong; this makes it a reassuring buy for the majority of customers. No wonder most “commercial” sauvignons are made in the same sort of style. I’m also tempted to believe that this factor is a part of the incredible international popularity of Burgundy (and increasingly now of Barolo), at the most rarefied critical levels downwards – and so of pinot noir and chardonnay from other parts of the world. (Hence the great commercial, and critical, success of the Hemel-en-Aarde.)

Another problem, obviously connected with the above, is that the response has widely been that if varietalism is good, then mono-varietalism must be better. Ask local retailers or any serious local producer of white blends about the commercial success of that category, although it is certainly one of the greatest glories of modern South African wine.

We do, admittedly, I’m pleased to say, have here a tradition for respecting red blends, especially the Bordeaux-style reds, and this is internationally uncommon. For many producers, the cab-based blend is traditionally the most prestigious wine in the portfolio, ahead of cabernet (Meerlust, Kanonkop, etc). That’s not generally the case elsewhere in the “New World” where varietalism rules. There are certainly some famous Californian blends which don’t have varietal names – but even some of these tend to be known as “cabernet sauvignon”. And many of the wines that are sold as Napa Cabernet Sauvignon are undeclared blends – with up to 25% of other varieties allowed. (I noticed, for example, this note about the prestigious Silver Oak Cabernet Sauvignon, from Napa: “If you take a look at the composition of our Cabernets side by side, you’ll notice that the Napa Valley Cabernet is more of a blend. There’s approximately 80 percent Cabernet Sauvignon compared to the 95+ percent Cabernet Sauvignon in the Alexander Valley Cabernet.”) Such is the prestige of the particular grape, and of monovarietal wine.

As so often, I’ve got a bit carried away, and haven’t left enough room to return to the question of the Sadie multi-blends. But I have been talking to Eben about them, and it really is a fascinating story and strategy; so I plan to pick up on that next week.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

The post Tim James: Varietal wines, mono-varietals, and multi-blends appeared first on winemag.

content:
Cape Grace Hotel has launched Terroir & Table, a new monthly dinner series pairing leading South African wine producers with seasonal menus at its restaurant, Heirloom.

The inaugural event took place on Saturday 25 July featuring Sam Lambson of Minimalist Wines, a range of cool-climate, site-specific Syrahs.

Guests enjoyed a four-course dinner by executive chef Wesli Jacobs, with Lambson hosting the evening and presenting the wines.

The series continues with:

Trizanne Signature Wines (29 August)

Heritage Weekend collaboration with VUUR’s Shaun Scrooby (25–26 September)

De Grendel (24 October)

To book, call +27 21 410 7100 or go to dineplan.com.

title: Greg Sherwood MW: Can SA’s fine wine progress continue in tougher times?
summary:
South Africa’s wine finds itself in a curious position at the moment as its exports to the UK, its single largest market, keep earning more money while shipping less liquid. So, after a long chat over the phone this week to a famous Stellenbosch producer, I thought it would be interesting to drill down on […]

The post Greg Sherwood MW: Can SA’s fine wine progress continue in tougher times? appeared first on winemag.
content:
South Africa’s wine finds itself in a curious position at the moment as its exports to the UK, its single largest market, keep earning more money while shipping less liquid. So, after a long chat over the phone this week to a famous Stellenbosch producer, I thought it would be interesting to drill down on this subject a little further, ahead of my upcoming trip to the Cape, as I am sure to be asked to offer further commentary on this topic.

Recent industry figures show that in 2025 the UK still accounted for roughly a fifth of South Africa’s total export value even as shipped volumes fell by around 6% to 7% year on year. Industry body Wines of South Africa (WOSA) has openly framed this shift as a deliberate strategy, to prioritise value over volume and retreat somewhat from the bargain-bin battlefield of bulk wine, preferring to fight for space on the fine wine shelves and listings in on-trade wine lists.

The question this raises is bigger than the trade statistics themselves. As European wine consumption contracts and the ageing cohort of serious collectors reportedly drift back towards Bordeaux, Burgundy, Piedmont and the Rhône, can South Africa’s premium category really establish itself as a peer to the old world’s classics, or is it destined to remain a well-regarded but secondary player in the fine wine market?

The backdrop: falling consumption, rising premiumisation

Certainly, looking around the UK market, the broader context is unforgiving. UK wine consumption supposedly peaked back in 2009, and has been sliding ever since, with overall alcohol volumes continuing to soften even as total market value edges up on premiumisation.

Younger drinkers are not replacing the older ones at anything like the same rate, with mindful drinking habits continuing to spread and ready-to-drink cocktails and No/Lo alcohol alternatives eating into wine’s share of the drinks trolley. Even wider afield in France, wine’s spiritual fine wine home, its market it not immune, with recent data showing still wine volumes falling there too, with the red wine category hardest hit.

In other words, South African is not competing in a growing market against entrenched incumbents, it is competing for a larger slice of a market that is itself getting smaller for almost everyone. Paradoxically, that shared pain is possibly part of what makes South Africa’s positioning more coherent.

If the market for cheap, everyday wine is contracting fastest as we are told, and if the surviving demand is concentrating in the premium and super premium tiers, then a producing country’s fortunes depend less on how many bottles it can push and more on whether its top wines are credible at the dinner table alongside a Claret, or a Chianti Classico. South Africa’s export strategy of smaller volumes at better price points is essentially a bet that its reputation for quality can carry it into that shrinking but higher-value space.

The case for a positive outlook

There is of course real substance behind those betting South Africa can and will compete. Regions like Stellenbosch, Swartland, Hemel-en-Aarde and Elgin have spent almost two decades building a track record with the critics and sommeliers, and South African Chenin Blanc, Cape Bordeaux Blends and cool-climate Syrah from various regions increasingly turn up on serious wine lists rather than as house pours.

According to recent export stats, bulk wine pricing has also actually been improving even as volumes fall, which suggests underlying quality is being rewarded rather than the country simply exporting less of the same commodity juice. South Africa also benefits from a currency that keeps its top wine competitively priced relative to Burgundy or Napa Valley equivalents of similar quality. This “quality per pound” argument definitely resonates with UK consumers who are increasingly becoming more price conscious than a decade ago, even at the premium fine wine end.

There is also a strong demographic argument emerging in South Africa’s favour, not just against it. The classic ageing UK collector base that I’ve worked amongst for several decades and that I often refer to in my articles, which is reported gravitating back to blue-chip Bordeaux and Burgundy, is by definition, a shrinking and eventually non-renewing customer group.

Meanwhile, the wine trade press has been fairly consistent in describing younger UK drinkers as wanting “stories in the glass” but also provenance, authenticity and a sense of discovery, rather than simply defaulting to whatever their parents drank. That is fertile ground for a New World country like South Africa, with a genuinely interesting story, post-apartheid transformation, old vine heritage, bio-diversity conscious regenerative viticulture in the Cape’s fynbos kingdom, and a first-generation of independent smallholder producers.

None of these factors guarantee sales of course, but it is a ‘narrative asset’ that the classic regions cannot easily replicate, precisely because their story is much more grounded in continuity rather than change.

The case to consider against South African wine

But as any producer will tell you, marketing, a well-established narrative and a value-for-money proposition only go so far against the centuries of institutional prestige hotwired into regions like Bordeaux and Burgundy. Fine wine, as an asset class as much as a beverage, trades heavily on scarcity, provenance chains, and also secondary market liquidity, the very things Bordeaux first growths and Grand Cru Burgundy have spent generations entrenching through classifications, negociant systems and an active auction and investment market.

Fine wine trading indices such as Liv-ex, tracking Bordeaux first growths have remained comparatively resilient even in a soft market, while wealthy buyers keep chasing rare, sought-after bottlings and Chinese and wider Asian demand shows tentative signs of returning for established names.

South African wines, however excellent, largely sit outside this investment ecosystem, with a few exceptions. A wine buyer nearing retirement age, reallocating a fine wine portfolio back towards “safe” classical names, is not really choosing between Stellenbosch Cabernet and a Pauillac Bordeaux Cru Classé based on taste alone, they are often buying reputational security, resale confidence and status signalling that many South African wines still simply do not have sufficiently.

There is also a structural fragility at home in South Africa, with a shrinking vineyard area, smaller harvests, and a domestic market under real economic pressure, helping to limit South Africa’s ability to consistently supply enough top-tier wine to seed that long-term prestige-building process – something, industry leaders like Mike Ratcliffe, have been opining about for years now.

Old world regions can lean on centuries of stock, library vintages and a self-reinforcing culture of collecting, while South Africa is still, relatively speaking, building up that new, post-apartheid era fine wine archive one vintage at a time.

A challenging global market but signs for optimism

As is normally the case in economic discussions like this, the honest answer is perhaps a little more nuanced than many commentators in Europe tend to let on – that South Africa’s premium wine category can compete but perhaps in a more specific and limited sense. It can absolutely win on the merits at the dinner table, in blind tastings (as I know all too well), and increasingly among sommeliers and adventurous drinkers who value quality and a story over simple ‘brand security.’

What it cannot yet do, at least not within a single generational cycle, is displace the old-world classics as the default choice of the risk-averse collector guarding their capital in a difficult economy.

As the market shrinks, South Africa’s realistic path to growth is not head-to-head combat with Bordeaux and Burgundy for the same conservative buyers, but capturing the more curious, value-conscious, and younger segment of a fine wine market that the classics are still, for the most part, too expensive by default.

South Africa’s premium producers simply need to become more proficient at operating in, and marketing to, these fine margins of the consumer fine wine category. Therein lies future long-term success.

  • Greg Sherwood was born in Pretoria, South Africa, and as the son of a career diplomat, spent his first 21 years traveling the globe with his parents. With a Business Management and Marketing degree from Webster University, St. Louis, Missouri, USA, Sherwood began his working career as a commodity trader. In 2000, he decided to make more of a long-held interest in wine taking a position at Handford Wines in South Kensington, London, working his way up to the position of Senior Wine Buyer over 22 years. Sherwood currently consults to a number of top fine wine merchants in London while always keeping one eye firmly on the South African wine industry. He qualified as the 303rd Master of Wine in 2007.
